claims.text: The starting as-cast CoCrFeNi alloy has a grain size of approximately 20 µm.
The starting as-cast CoCrFeNi alloy has a hardness of approximately 200 HV.
The starting CoCrFeNi alloy contains no solid-lubricant phases.
Blending 15 vol% CaF2 microparticles with CoCrFeNi and hot pressing at 1000 °C followed by a 2 h anneal will produce a uniform composite.
Sliding of the CoCrFeNi–15 vol% CaF2 composite will generate a continuous CaF2-rich tribofilm.
Contact stress and thermal activation cause CaF2 particles to extrude and plastically deform at the sliding surface.
The deformed CaF2 particles form a low-shear-strength fluoride layer.
The CaF2-rich fluoride layer is stable up to 800 °C.
The CaF2-rich tribofilm separates or decouples metallic asperity contacts.
Decoupling metallic asperity contacts lowers both friction and wear.
The composite will maintain a coefficient of friction below 0.3 throughout 25–800 °C at loads of 1–20 N in both air and Ar.
The composite will maintain a wear rate below 5×10^-6 mm^3/Nm throughout 25–800 °C.
Adding 15 vol% CaF2 will reduce wear by at least 50% relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi has a room-temperature coefficient of friction of approximately 0.6 under similar test conditions.
The coefficient of friction of unmodified CoCrFeNi rises to approximately 0.8 at 800 °C under similar test conditions.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi has a wear rate of approximately 1×10^-5 mm^3/Nm under similar test conditions.
Above approximately 700 °C in air, oxidation of CaF2 may degrade the tribofilm.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires coefficient of friction below 0.3, but the stated rule only falsifies it above 0.5. Results between 0.3 and 0.5 would contradict the prediction without meeting the falsification rule.

The predicted wear-rate ceiling is 5×10^-6 mm^3/Nm, whereas falsification requires exceeding 1×10^-5 mm^3/Nm. A result between these values would violate the hypothesis but not falsify it under the stated rule.

The mechanism categorically describes the fluoride layer as stable to 800 °C and the boundary includes air to 800 °C, while the uncertainty states that oxidation may degrade the film above about 700 °C in air.
